cues.text: Section nine is about measuring strategic IT value.
Let us begin with key performance indicators, or KPIs.
KPIs are indicators that are tied to objectives.
That tie matters: a number is only a KPI when it tells you how well you are progressing toward something the organisation is trying to achieve.

Depending on what is appropriate, you may track return on investment, or ROI; operating costs; customer satisfaction; response time; service availability; process cycle time; error rate; adoption; revenue contribution; and employee capability.
Notice how this list spans finance, customers, operations, and people.
No single organisation needs all of them, so you choose the ones that fit your objectives.
The source then adds an important management point.
A metric without a target and an accountable owner is difficult to manage.
Think about why.
Without a target, you cannot say whether a result is good or bad.
Without an owner, nobody is responsible for acting when the number moves in the wrong direction.
So every metric should come with both a target and a named person who is accountable for it.
Next, the source asks us to distinguish output from outcome.
An output is what you produce or deliver.
An outcome is the change in business results that follows.
The example given is this: launching a chatbot is an output.
Reducing customer waiting time while maintaining satisfaction is an outcome.
The launch tells you that something was delivered.
The outcome tells you whether it actually helped customers, and notice that the outcome includes a qualification, which is that satisfaction must be maintained.
Faster responses that leave customers unhappy would not count as success.
To measure outcomes properly, the source gives a sequence of steps.
First, establish a baseline before implementation, so you know where you started.
Second, set targets, so you know what improvement you are aiming for.
Third, monitor trends over time, rather than relying on a single reading.
And fourth, investigate unintended effects, because a change can produce side effects that nobody planned for, whether good or bad.
Finally, the source warns us to avoid vanity metrics.
Its example is the number of features deployed.
Such a figure may look impressive, but when it does not demonstrate business value, it tells you very little.
The test is always whether the metric shows that the organisation is better off, not merely that more work was delivered.

To summarise this section: choose KPIs linked to objectives, give each a target and an accountable owner, measure outcomes rather than only outputs, set a baseline first, watch trends and side effects, and steer clear of vanity metrics.
